solution-particle-models-s1.title: Four drawings of sodium chloride in water
solution-particle-models-s1.html: Key: blue +, Na⁺; green −, Cl⁻; orange circle, oxygen; white circle, hydrogen.

solution-particle-models-s2.title: A potassium sulfate solution
solution-particle-models-s2.html: Key: blue +, K⁺; yellow center with four orange O, SO₄²⁻ (water molecules not shown).

items.q: Which box correctly represents NaCl dissolved in water?
options: W
X
Y
Z

why.correct: W shows separate ions in a 1 : 1 ratio, with water's δ− oxygen toward Na⁺ and a δ+ hydrogen toward Cl⁻.
options: Right: separate ions, 1 : 1, correct orientation.
X has every water molecule backwards: H toward the cation and O toward the anion, so like charges face each other.
Y shows the ions still paired, but dissolving separates them into hydrated ions.
Z shows two Na⁺ for one Cl⁻, which has a net charge of +1 and the wrong ratio for NaCl.

items.q: What is wrong with box X?
options: Like partial charges face each other: water's δ+ H points at Na⁺ and its δ− O at Cl⁻.
It shows the ions separated, but in water the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions stay bonded together.
It has too many water molecules, because each ion attracts one water molecule.
It shows Cl⁻ as larger than Na⁺, but the chloride ion is the smaller of the two.

why.correct: Ion-dipole attraction lines up opposite charges. X turns every water molecule backwards, which would put repelling charges side by side.
options: Right: the orientation is reversed for both ions.
Dissolving does separate the ions; that part of X is correct.
Each ion is surrounded by several water molecules, so a shell of four is reasonable.
Cl⁻ (181 pm) is larger than Na⁺ (102 pm), as drawn.

items.q: Why is box Y not a correct picture of the solution?
options: Dissolving separates the ions, and each ion is hydrated; Y shows an ion pair that has not come apart.
Y has too few water molecules in it to represent water as the solvent for the solution.
Y shows the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in a 1 : 1 ratio, but the ratio in the solution is 2 : 1.
Y shows covalent bonds inside the water molecules, which break when salt dissolves in water.

why.correct: Ion-dipole attractions pull the ions out of the lattice and apart. A correct drawing shows each ion separately, with its own water shell.
options: Right: the ions should be separate and hydrated.
Y shows several water molecules; the number drawn is a sampling choice.
NaCl gives a 1 : 1 ratio, which Y gets right.
The O–H bonds in water do not break when salt dissolves.

items.q: Box Z has the water oriented correctly. What error does it make?
options: It has a net charge of +1, because there are two Na⁺ for one Cl⁻ instead of a 1 : 1 ratio.
It shows the Na⁺ ions hydrated, but a cation is not surrounded by water molecules.
It spreads the ions through the box, but dissolved ions settle at the bottom of the box.
It shows Na⁺ and Cl⁻ separated, but NaCl dissolves as molecules, not as ions.

why.correct: NaCl is 1 : 1, so any box of NaCl(aq) has equal numbers of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and a total charge of zero.
options: Right: the formula ratio, and the charge balance, are wrong.
Cations are hydrated too, with water's O pointing in.
A solution is homogeneous, so ions spread through it.
NaCl is ionic and separates into ions.

items.q: How many solute particles (ions) are shown in the box?

mistakes.why: Value: you counted each sulfur and oxygen atom separately. A sulfate ion is one particle; its covalent bonds do not break.

why.correct: Three SO₄²⁻ ions and six K⁺ ions: 3 + 6 = 9 ions. Each sulfate ion counts as one particle; its atoms stay bonded together.

items.q: Why does the drawing show twice as many K⁺ ions as SO₄²⁻ ions?
options: K₂SO₄ gives two K⁺ for each SO₄²⁻, so the charges balance: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0.
K⁺ ions are smaller, so more of them fit into the same volume of the solution.
Half of the sulfate ions break apart into sulfur and oxygen atoms when dissolved.
Potassium ions attract more water, so more of them dissolve than sulfate ions.

why.correct: The formula K₂SO₄ fixes the ratio: two K⁺ per SO₄²⁻, which makes each formula unit, and the whole box, neutral.
options: Right: the ratio follows the formula and the charges.
Ion size does not set how many of each ion form.
Sulfate stays whole; the S–O bonds are covalent.
Every formula unit gives the same two K⁺ and one SO₄²⁻.

items.q: Water molecules are added to the drawing around one K⁺ ion and one SO₄²⁻ ion. How should they point?
options: O toward K⁺; H toward the O atoms of SO₄²⁻.
H toward K⁺; O toward the O atoms of SO₄²⁻.
O toward both ions, because oxygen is the larger atom.
H toward both ions, because hydrogen bonds to both.

why.correct: Opposite charges face each other: water's δ− oxygen toward the cation, and its δ+ hydrogens toward the negatively charged sulfate ion (whose outer O atoms carry the negative charge).
options: Right: δ− to the cation, δ+ to the anion.
This reverses both: like charges would face each other.
Atom size does not decide; charge does, and O is δ− so it suits only the cation.
H is δ+, so it is attracted to the anion but repelled by the cation.

items.q: If the box represents 0.150 M K₂SO₄, what is the molarity of K⁺ ions?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the molarity of K₂SO₄ itself. Each formula unit releases two K⁺ ions.
Value: you halved it. There are twice as many K⁺ ions as formula units, so double.

why.correct: Each K₂SO₄ gives two K⁺, so [K⁺] = 2 × 0.150 M = 0.300 M.

items.q: Which ion attracts the water molecules around it most strongly?
options: Mg²⁺ (radius 72 pm)
Na⁺ (radius 102 pm)
K⁺ (radius 138 pm)
Ca²⁺ (radius 100 pm)

why.correct: By Coulomb's law the attraction grows with charge and falls with distance. Mg²⁺ has the larger charge (2+) and the smallest radius, so water molecules can get closest to the most charge.
options: Right: high charge, small radius.
Na⁺ has only a 1+ charge and a larger radius than Mg²⁺.
K⁺ has a 1+ charge and the largest radius.
Ca²⁺ has the same charge as Mg²⁺ but a larger radius, so water sits farther away.

items.q: Which particle diagram describes an aqueous solution of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆?
options: Whole glucose molecules spread among water molecules
Separate C, H and O atoms spread among water molecules
Glucose⁺ and glucose⁻ ions surrounded by water
Glucose molecules piled in a layer at the bottom

why.correct: Glucose is a molecular compound. It dissolves as intact molecules held among the water molecules by hydrogen bonds; it forms no ions.
options: Right: intact molecules, evenly spread.
Dissolving does not break covalent bonds; the molecules stay whole.
Glucose is not ionic and does not form ions.
A solution is homogeneous, so the molecules spread evenly.

items.q: A correct particle diagram of 0.10 M Ca(NO₃)₂(aq) shows which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: Two NO₃⁻ ions for every Ca²⁺ ion
Each NO₃⁻ ion drawn as one N bonded to three O
Ca²⁺ ions with water hydrogens pointing toward them
Separate N and O atoms from broken nitrate ions
Ions spread evenly through the box
Ca(NO₃)₂ units with the ions still touching

why.correct: Ca(NO₃)₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2 NO₃⁻. Nitrate ions stay whole, the ions spread evenly, and water's oxygen (not hydrogen) points at Ca²⁺.
options: Right: the formula ratio is 1 : 2.
Right: polyatomic ions keep their covalent bonds.
Water's δ+ hydrogens would be repelled by a cation; the oxygen points in.
Nitrate stays whole when the salt dissolves.
Right: a solution is homogeneous.
Dissolving separates the ions; they do not stay as formula units.

items.q: A student draws dissolved KBr with each water molecule's oxygen pointing toward BOTH the K⁺ and the Br⁻ ions, "because oxygen is the part of water that bonds." Which response is best?
options: Water orients by charge: δ− O faces K⁺, but δ+ H must face Br⁻, since O facing Br⁻ would repel.
The drawing is correct, because the oxygen atom forms hydrogen bonds with the ions in solution.
The drawing is correct for K⁺ and Br⁻ alike, because both are ions with a full charge on them.
Water should point H toward both ions, because H is the δ+ end and so it attracts ions.

why.correct: Ion-dipole attraction is Coulombic. A δ− oxygen is attracted to a cation and repelled by an anion, so around Br⁻ the water molecules turn their δ+ hydrogens inward.
options: Right: orientation depends on the ion's sign.
Ion-dipole forces are not hydrogen bonds, and O–to–anion would repel.
A full charge of either sign attracts the opposite end of water, which differs for + and −.
δ+ H would be repelled by K⁺.

items.q: Each box below represents equal volumes of 0.20 M solutions. Which solution has the most solute particles in the box?
options: 0.20 M AlCl₃
0.20 M NaCl
0.20 M MgSO₄
0.20 M sucrose

why.correct: AlCl₃ → Al³⁺ + 3 Cl⁻ gives 4 ions per formula unit (0.80 M of particles). NaCl and MgSO₄ give 2 each (0.40 M), and sucrose gives 1 molecule (0.20 M).
options: Right: four ions per formula unit.
Two ions per formula unit.
Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻: two ions per formula unit.
Sucrose stays as whole molecules: one particle each.

items.q: A box representing a solution of FeCl₃ shows 12 chloride ions. How many iron(III) ions should it show?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied by 3. There are three Cl⁻ for each Fe³⁺, so divide.
Value: the ratio is not 1 : 1. FeCl₃ gives three Cl⁻ per Fe³⁺.

why.correct: FeCl₃ → Fe³⁺ + 3 Cl⁻, so there is one Fe³⁺ per three Cl⁻: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Fe³⁺. Check: 4(+3) + 12(−1) = 0.

items.q: Solid KCl is added to water and stirred until it has all dissolved. Which change at the particle level allows the solution to conduct electricity?
options: The K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions separate and can move independently through the water.
The K–Cl covalent bonds break, releasing free electrons that carry the current.
Water molecules break into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions when they touch the KCl crystal.
The KCl units stay together but become polar, so they line up with the current.

why.correct: In the solid the ions are fixed in place. Dissolving separates them into hydrated ions that can move, and moving charged particles carry a current.
options: Right: mobile ions carry the current.
KCl is ionic, not covalent, and no free electrons are released.
Water stays as H₂O molecules; the ions come from the KCl.
The ions separate rather than staying together as KCl units.
